paragraphs: This paper develops an algorithm for learning a generalized factorization machine from streaming data. The model includes a matrix of second-order coefficients, which describes interactions between input features. The approach alternates between estimation steps while processing the dataset once, making its storage requirements especially relevant when examples arrive continuously.

The recovery guarantees depend on explicit assumptions: inputs are random Gaussian vectors in d dimensions, and the target coefficient matrix has rank k. Under these conditions, the algorithm converges linearly and reaches O(ε) recovery error using O(k³d log(1/ε)) training examples. It needs O(kd) memory, and each iteration uses matrix-vector products.

The theoretical construction is an estimation sequence satisfying a condition called conditionally independent RIP. This condition supports the analysis of the alternating procedure. The framework also covers symmetric and asymmetric rank-one matrix sensing as special cases, connecting the result to inductive matrix completion and phase retrieval. Its contribution combines a streaming implementation with recovery guarantees for the stated data model.
neurips-2016-a-non-convex-one-pass-frame.tldr: A one-pass alternating algorithm learns generalized factorization machines with efficient memory use and provable recovery under Gaussian-input and low-rank assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to estimate a patient's clinical condition from several physiological measurements collected concurrently. Such estimates can inform whether an intervention is needed and how patients should be prioritized. The challenge is to turn multiple changing streams into a timely assessment whose accuracy can be supported statistically.

The authors construct a non-parametric learning algorithm that combines Bayesian inference, permutation testing, and generalizations of the empirical Bernstein inequality. The combination targets three issues together: bias caused by therapeutic intervention censoring, delays in producing sufficiently accurate estimates, and detection of anomalous clinical states. Intervention censoring matters because treatment affects which observations remain available for estimating the patient's condition.

The algorithm is validated on real patient data from a cancer ward in a large academic hospital. The stated contribution is therefore a method addressing several connected estimation problems, supported by a clinical-data evaluation. Its emphasis on timeliness alongside accuracy makes confidence in an estimate part of the learning problem, rather than treating speed and reliability as unrelated goals.
neurips-2016-a-non-parametric-learning-m.tldr: A non-parametric algorithm combines statistical tools to estimate clinical state promptly, address intervention-related bias, and detect anomalies.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs missing entries from a partially observed matrix. This paper uses additional features describing its rows and columns to make that reconstruction more efficient. Its sparse model explicitly represents interactions between these two sets of features, without requiring the model's parameter matrix to have low rank.

The strongest recovery result depends on the quality of the side information. When those features span the matrix's latent feature space, exact recovery requires O(log N) observed entries, where N denotes matrix size. When the side features are slightly perturbed latent features, the method instead supports ε-accurate recovery with the same logarithmic sample complexity. These statements link recovery efficiency to how well the supplied features capture the underlying structure.

The authors also develop a linearized Lagrangian algorithm with a strong convergence guarantee. In simulations and real datasets, the approach outperforms three methods described as state of the art. The contribution brings together an interaction-based sparse formulation, conditional recovery theory, and an efficient optimization procedure.
neurips-2016-a-sparse-interactive-model-.tldr: A sparse interaction model uses row and column features for matrix completion, with logarithmic sample requirements when the side information sufficiently captures latent structure.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks can overfit their training data, and the abstract identifies ordinary applications of dropout to recurrent layers as unsuccessful. This creates a practical problem: a regularization technique useful elsewhere in deep learning cannot simply be carried over without considering the recurrent model's structure.

The paper derives a dropout technique from a Bayesian interpretation of neural-network training. In this view, dropout relates to approximate Bayesian inference, and extending that reasoning to recurrent models suggests a variational inference approach to regularization. The theory therefore serves as a guide for constructing the method, rather than only as an explanation after its design.

The authors evaluate the approach in LSTM and GRU networks on language modelling and sentiment analysis. They report improvements over existing techniques and a Penn Treebank test perplexity of 73.4, described, to their knowledge, as an improvement on the single-model state of the art. These results support the usefulness of the proposed Bayesian grounding for recurrent-network regularization in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2016-a-theoretically-grounded-ap.tldr: A variational inference interpretation of dropout yields a recurrent-network regularizer that improves the evaluated language and sentiment models.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing systems often assign new tasks using the answers already collected, so spending can respond to emerging evidence. Yet earlier theoretical analyses suggested that this adaptivity offered little benefit. The paper investigates whether that conclusion changes under a more general probabilistic model designed to describe practical crowdsourcing data.

Working within a generalized Dawid-Skene model, the authors characterize the fundamental relationship between available budget and achievable accuracy. They then construct an adaptive assignment scheme that matches this limit. Budget optimality here is a statement within that model: the scheme reaches the performance boundary established by the analysis.

The authors compare this boundary with the corresponding one for assignments fixed without adaptation. They find that the advantage of adaptivity can be significant and can become arbitrarily large, depending on the distribution of task difficulty. This dependence is central to the result. It explains how adaptive allocation can have substantial value in some crowdsourcing settings even when less general analyses predict only small gains.
neurips-2016-achieving-budget-optimality.tldr: Under a generalized crowdsourcing model, an adaptive assignment scheme attains the optimal budget–accuracy trade-off and can greatly outperform non-adaptive allocation.

paragraphs: Bayesian minimum mean squared error inference can require difficult integration, so maximum a posteriori estimation is often used as a computational substitute. The paper examines a high-dimensional regime where parameter counts and sample counts have comparable scale. In this setting, the abstract identifies the accuracy of the usual substitute as suboptimal.

The authors show how an appropriately chosen convex penalty and regularization function can make optimization asymptotically achieve minimum mean squared error performance. These choices form a smoothed version of the commonly used maximum a posteriori approach. The equivalence concerns achievable inference performance in the analyzed high-dimensional limit, rather than an unrestricted identity between every Bayesian integral and optimization problem.

The findings give a new derivation and interpretation of previously discovered optimal M-estimators and extend the treatment to non-additive noise models. Numerical simulations demonstrate the estimators' performance. The central significance is computational: under the paper's framework, a carefully designed convex optimization problem can reach the asymptotic accuracy associated with a more demanding Bayesian calculation.
neurips-2016-an-equivalence-between-high.tldr: Appropriately designed convex estimators can asymptotically attain Bayes-optimal mean squared error in the high-dimensional setting studied.

paragraphs: The maximum-entropy principle selects a distribution that matches specified averages while retaining as much uncertainty as possible. Although the resulting distribution belongs to an exponential family, finding its parameters can be computationally intractable. This paper develops an efficient approximate version when the supplied information consists of pairwise moments.

The constructed distributions approximately reproduce those moments while achieving entropy comparable to that of the exact maximum-entropy solution. Both parts matter: matching the statistics alone would not preserve the uncertainty objective, while high entropy alone would not respect the observed relationships. The result provides a computationally accessible way to pursue these requirements together.

The authors apply this principle to variational calculations for the log-partition function of Ising models. Their approximation guarantees require no assumptions on the models' potentials. They obtain guarantees comparable to those available in the low-temperature limit, where the related problem becomes optimization of quadratic forms over the hypercube. This connects an approximate distribution-construction principle to provable methods for a difficult probabilistic calculation.
neurips-2016-approximate-maximum-entropy.tldr: Efficient approximate maximum-entropy constructions yield provable variational guarantees for Ising log-partition functions without restrictions on model potentials.

paragraphs: Calcium imaging allows researchers to monitor the activity of thousands of neurons at once. As these datasets grow, identifying the individual neurons becomes an increasingly important task to automate. This paper treats neuron detection as a supervised learning problem and applies convolutional networks to the imaging data.

The evaluation compares detected neurons with annotations supplied by a human expert. Precision and recall provide the basis for assessing accuracy: they reflect how reliably detections correspond to annotated neurons and how many annotated neurons are found. On these measures, the convolutional-network approach performs better than the popular PCA/ICA method.

The authors report accuracy approaching human performance together with speed exceeding human performance. Those findings address two practical demands of large-scale analysis: preserving the quality of neuron identification and reducing the time needed to carry it out. The results suggest that convolutional networks offer an efficient and flexible tool for calcium-imaging analysis, with the stated accuracy comparison grounded specifically in expert-provided annotations.
neurips-2016-automatic-neuron-detection-.tldr: Supervised convolutional networks detect neurons in calcium images with reported near-human accuracy, faster-than-human speed, and better precision and recall than PCA/ICA.

paragraphs: This paper studies crowdsourcing when workers evaluate items produced by other workers and some ratings may be deliberately misleading. Among n workers, an unknown fraction α supplies reliable ratings; everyone else may behave arbitrarily. A manager can inspect a small number of items directly and wants to recover almost all high-quality items while keeping low-quality inclusions limited.

The main result is that this curation can be achieved without the stated workload for the manager or each individual worker scaling with n. The bounds instead depend on the reliable-worker fraction, the high-quality-item fraction β, and an error parameter ε. The respective bounds are expressed as Õ(1/(βαε⁴)) ratings per worker and Õ(1/(βε²)) ratings by the manager.

The distinction between individual and total effort matters: the result concerns each worker's burden and the manager's burden as the collection grows. It demonstrates how limited direct evaluation can support curation despite an unknown adversarial population. The authors also extend their results to peer prediction, including peer grading in online classrooms.
neurips-2016-avoiding-imposters-and-deli.tldr: With a reliable fraction of workers and limited manager checks, adversarial crowdsourcing permits accurate curation with individual workloads that do not scale with collection size.

paragraphs: The paper develops a Bayesian forecasting method for large e-commerce inventories, with particular attention to demand that is intermittent or arrives in bursts. These patterns make forecasting more than a matter of following a smoothly changing sales level. The proposed method aims to handle such demand while remaining practical at the scale of a large platform.

Its computational contribution is an approximation to inference using Newton-Raphson updates reduced to linear-time Kalman smoothing. This reduction makes the inference procedure scalable: the authors report handling problems several orders of magnitude larger than those addressed by earlier related work. The method's practicality therefore depends on how the Bayesian calculation is organized, as well as on the forecasting approach itself.

The evaluation uses large real-world sales datasets. On fast- and medium-moving products, the method outperforms competing approaches. This is the stated empirical performance claim, even though intermittent and bursty demand motivates the broader design. Together, the computational and forecasting findings support using the approach for large inventories with varied sales patterns.
neurips-2016-bayesian-intermittent-deman.tldr: A scalable Bayesian demand forecaster uses linear-time Kalman smoothing and outperforms competing approaches on fast- and medium-moving items in large sales datasets.

paragraphs: Online allocation requires assigning resources before future requests are known. When there are two objectives, each decision must also navigate competing measures of success. The paper is motivated by applications such as advertising, where clicks, conversions, impressions, and other measures can create distinct allocation priorities.

The authors study allocating items to agents with two submodular value functions. Submodularity captures diminishing returns, so the value of another allocation depends on what has already been assigned. They establish almost matching upper and lower bounds for this online problem, addressing a setting where the input may be adversarial rather than conveniently predictable.

The closeness of the bounds means that the algorithms' guarantees approach the limits established for the problem. The paper also examines special cases relevant to internet advertising and obtains improved results there. The authors describe the algorithms as efficient and straightforward to implement. The contribution is a theoretical account of what can be achieved when uncertain future arrivals and two allocation objectives must be handled together.
neurips-2016-bi-objective-online-matchin.tldr: The paper develops nearly optimal algorithms and bounds for online allocation with two submodular objectives, including advertising-related special cases.

paragraphs: Active learning reduces annotation effort by choosing which unlabeled examples should receive labels. Methods that choose from an available pool can use utility functions with adaptive submodularity to obtain theoretical guarantees. The paper addresses the less developed streaming setting, where examples arrive over time and selection must operate within that flow.

The authors introduce policy-adaptive submodular functions, a new class of utility functions. They prove that the class includes many existing adaptive submodular functions used in real-world problems. This inclusion matters because it makes the new framework applicable to established choices of learning utility, rather than requiring every streaming method to start from a separate objective.

Using this property, the framework converts existing pool-based methods into stream-based methods and supplies performance guarantees. The authors also compare the resulting methods with existing heuristics on common benchmark datasets, reporting empirical effectiveness. The contribution thus links a mathematical generalization to a practical transfer: methods designed for selecting from a pool can support budgeted decisions over a stream.
neurips-2016-budgeted-stream-based-activ.tldr: Policy-adaptive submodularity provides a framework for converting pool-based active learning methods into streaming methods with performance guarantees.

paragraphs: Choosing a convolutional-network architecture is itself a difficult design problem. This paper proposes a neural fabric that contains exponentially many possible architectures within one connected structure. Its aim is to make a broad collection of architectural choices available inside a model that can be trained through standard methods.

The fabric is a three-dimensional trellis connecting response maps across layers, scales, and channels through a sparse, uniform pattern of local connections. Individual architectures correspond to paths through that trellis. The structure can also combine all embedded architectures as an ensemble, sharing parameters wherever their paths overlap. Its stated architectural hyperparameters are the numbers of layers and channels.

Training uses back-propagation, with cost growing linearly in the size of the fabric. The authors report results competitive with the state of the art on MNIST and CIFAR10 image classification and Part Labels semantic segmentation. These findings support the practicality of representing many architectures through a shared structure without separately training every architecture it contains.
neurips-2016-convolutional-neural-fabric.tldr: Neural fabrics embed and jointly train exponentially many convolutional architectures through a sparse shared structure, achieving competitive classification and segmentation results.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks commonly operate on regular grids, such as the pixels of an image. Many other datasets have irregular relationships better represented by graphs, including social networks and brain connections. This paper develops a way to bring convolutional learning to those graph domains while preserving efficient local filtering.

The formulation uses spectral graph theory to define the filters and the numerical procedures that apply them. The proposed technique works with any graph structure and has the same stated linear computational complexity and constant learning complexity as classical convolutional networks. The significance is that irregular connectivity can be incorporated without giving up the complexity properties emphasized by the authors.

Experiments on MNIST and 20NEWS demonstrate learning of local, stationary, and compositional graph features. These properties concern patterns associated with neighborhoods, reused across locations, and combined into richer representations. The findings support the paper's central claim that the useful feature-building behavior of convolutional networks can extend beyond regular grids to data organized by graph relationships.
neurips-2016-convolutional-neural-networ.tldr: A spectral formulation extends convolutional networks to arbitrary graphs using efficient localized filters and demonstrates graph-based feature learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies language learning through conversation, where a partner's response supplies supervision implicitly. This differs from training entirely on fixed collections of explicitly labeled words or sentences. The motivation is that communication can itself provide information for learning, rather than serving only as an activity performed after training.

The authors examine this setting in the bAbI domain and in large-scale question answering. They evaluate baseline learning strategies and introduce a model with predictive lookahead. Its learning approach incorporates anticipation of the teacher's response, making that response a useful source of information about how to answer questions.

The model is reported as promising for learning from conversational feedback. A particularly striking finding is that it can learn correct answers without reward-based supervision. That result still involves supervision through the teacher's responses; the information arrives through language rather than a reward signal. The experiments therefore support conversational response prediction as a way to extract learning signals from an interaction itself.
neurips-2016-dialog-based-language-learn.tldr: A predictive-lookahead model learns from a teacher's conversational responses and can answer questions correctly without reward-based supervision in the studied tasks.

paragraphs: Word embeddings represent relationships among words through learned vectors. This paper extends that idea to other high-dimensional observations, including real-valued neural activity, shopping counts, and movie ratings. The framework models each observation using latent embeddings together with a context made up of other relevant observations.

Context depends on the application: nearby neurons can provide context for neural activity, while other products in a cart provide context for a shopping item. Each model specifies that context, an exponential-family conditional distribution, and how embedding vectors are shared across the data. Stochastic gradient descent fits the embeddings through an algorithm closely connected to generalized linear models.

The authors evaluate the framework on zebrafish neural activity, shopping behavior, and movie ratings. Across all three applications, the embedding models reconstruct held-out observations better than the other dimension-reduction methods evaluated and reveal interesting qualitative structure. The contribution is a reusable modelling recipe that adapts both the observation distribution and the meaning of context to the data.
neurips-2016-exponential-family-embeddin.tldr: Exponential family embeddings generalize context-based word representations to neural, shopping, and ratings data, improving held-out reconstruction in the three evaluated applications.

paragraphs: The paper considers personalized summaries built from two kinds of information: public data available to everyone and private data belonging to an individual user. A compact shared summary should support diverse public content, while each user's private contributions enable personalization without being shared with other users.

The formulation assumes that a user's summary utility is submodular, capturing diminishing returns from additional content. Personalized summarization then becomes a submodular cover problem. Running a centralized greedy procedure separately for every user is too costly at the scale considered. FASTCOVER instead uses a distributed algorithm to produce a compact summary for all users in one operation.

The authors show that FASTCOVER produces solutions competitive with a centralized algorithm while requiring exponentially fewer rounds than previous state-of-the-art results. A Spark implementation demonstrates practical performance for personalized location and movie recommendations, as well as dominating-set problems, on tens of millions of data points. The contribution makes the shared computation reusable across users under the stated utility assumption.
neurips-2016-fast-distributed-submodular.tldr: FASTCOVER efficiently builds shared summaries for public-private personalization, with competitive submodular-cover solutions and substantially fewer distributed rounds.

paragraphs: When a dataset has many features, potentially useful associations may involve combinations of them. Examining arbitrary combinations creates a search space of size 2^p for p features. The paper addresses an additional statistical challenge: checking whether a combination remains associated with a target after accounting for a categorical covariate that could confound the relationship.

The proposed Fast Automatic Conditional Search algorithm, or FACS, performs significant discriminative itemset mining while conditioning on categorical covariates. It builds on the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test. The stated O(k log k) scaling concerns k, the number of categories of the covariate, giving an efficient way to incorporate that conditioning into the search.

On simulated and real-world datasets, FACS shows better speed and statistical power than the compared state-of-the-art methods. These results matter because searching feature combinations and controlling for a potential confounder are both necessary parts of the intended analysis. The authors identify biomedical applications as a promising use for this ability to discover conditionally significant combinations.
neurips-2016-finding-significant-combina.tldr: FACS efficiently searches for significant feature combinations while conditioning on categorical covariates, improving speed and statistical power in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper uses unlabeled video to learn how scenes change over time. The goal covers both generating moving scenes and learning representations useful for recognizing actions. That connection makes temporal change a potential training signal even when videos lack detailed human-provided labels.

The proposed video generative adversarial network uses convolutions across space and time and separates the scene's foreground from its background. This organization provides a way to model scene dynamics within a video generator. The authors also use the model to predict plausible future motion from a static image.

Experiments suggest that the model produces tiny videos lasting up to one second at full frame rate better than simple baselines. Experiments and visualizations further show useful internal features for action recognition with minimal supervision. These findings support the possibility that learning to generate scene dynamics can also help representation learning. The stated generation result concerns short, tiny videos, while broader applications in video understanding and simulation are presented as potential impacts.
neurips-2016-generating-videos-with-scen.tldr: A foreground-background video GAN learns from unlabeled videos, generates short plausible clips, and develops features useful for minimally supervised action recognition.

paragraphs: Image classification, object detection, and boundary extraction are often treated as separate perceptual tasks. This paper asks how a neural network can solve such problems together efficiently and coherently. It explores both representations useful across tasks and a mechanism through which the tasks' solutions can inform one another.

The proposed architecture, called multinet, shares deep image features but also lets tasks interact recurrently. Each task encodes the results of its analysis into a common representation of the image. This shared representation therefore contains information from task outputs as well as the image features used to produce them.

On standard benchmarks, the authors show that sharing features improves individual-task performance and that integrating task solutions yields a larger improvement. The evidence supports interaction among perceptual tasks as a useful addition to common feature extraction. While universal image representations motivate the work, the reported finding is the improvement obtained by sharing and recurrently integrating information across the tasks evaluated.
neurips-2016-integrated-perception-with-.tldr: Multinet improves perceptual tasks by sharing image features and recurrently integrating task outputs into a common representation.

paragraphs: A statistical test can indicate that two distributions differ without making the difference easy to understand. This paper proposes two ways to measure distribution differences using a small collection of features at spatial or frequency locations. Each measure combines differences in expected values of analytic functions evaluated at those locations.

The features are selected by optimizing a lower bound on test power, the ability of a test to detect a difference when one exists. This connects interpretability with the test's statistical purpose: the chosen features should both expose local differences and help distinguish the distributions. The empirical criterion converges as sample size increases, supporting the quality of feature selection.

In benchmarks involving high-dimensional text and image data, the resulting tests run in linear time and achieve performance comparable to a state-of-the-art quadratic-time maximum mean discrepancy test. They also return features that people can interpret to understand the result. The contribution combines an efficient distribution test with a concise indication of where or how the distributions differ.
neurips-2016-interpretable-distribution-.tldr: Optimizing interpretable distribution features yields linear-time tests with benchmark performance comparable to quadratic-time maximum mean discrepancy testing.

paragraphs: Stochastic-gradient Markov chain Monte Carlo methods make Bayesian inference practical for large datasets, but bias can limit their accuracy. This paper proposes reducing that bias while keeping variance at a reasonable level. Its approach uses Richardson-Romberg extrapolation, a numerical technique for improving an approximation through calculations at different resolutions.

The construction runs nearly the same sampling algorithm twice in parallel with different step sizes. Applied to stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, it produces a method called SGRRLD. This offers a route to improved accuracy through paired runs of a familiar sampler, with the theoretical analysis addressing the behavior of their combined estimator.

The authors establish asymptotic consistency, a central limit theorem, and finite-time bounds on bias and mean squared error. They show higher convergence rates than SGLD both at finite times and asymptotically, attaining the theoretical accuracy of methods using higher-order integrators. Synthetic and real-data experiments support the findings. The contribution ties a relatively simple sampling construction to stronger accuracy guarantees.
neurips-2016-stochastic-gradient-richard.tldr: Combining stochastic-gradient Langevin runs at different step sizes reduces bias and yields stronger convergence guarantees through Richardson-Romberg extrapolation.

paragraphs: The threshold-bandit problem changes how an action earns a reward. On each round, the learner selects one of K actions, which draws a random sample from a fixed distribution. The learner earns a unit reward only if that sample exceeds a threshold supplied as side information.

The paper distinguishes two feedback settings. In the uncensored version, the learner always sees the sample. In the censored version, the sample is visible only when it fails to meet the threshold. These observation rules matter because the learner must use past feedback to decide which actions are likely to succeed at subsequent thresholds.

Using new analytical tools for the UCB algorithm, the authors show that the uncensored setting is essentially no harder than the classical multi-armed bandit problem. Censoring introduces additional challenges, and the paper supplies guarantees when threshold values are generated optimistically. Thus, the positive result for censored feedback depends on the stated threshold-generation condition, while the uncensored analysis establishes a closer connection to standard bandit learning.
neurips-2016-threshold-bandits-with-and-.tldr: Threshold bandits remain essentially as tractable as classical bandits with full sample feedback, while censored-feedback guarantees require optimistic threshold generation.

paragraphs: Variational methods approximate difficult posterior distributions or normalization constants in latent-variable models. Although often useful, their approximation error can be arbitrarily large. This paper addresses that concern by constructing a new class of bounds on the marginal log-likelihood of directed latent-variable models.

The method uses random projections to simplify the posterior. Its distinguishing theoretical claim is that the resulting bounds are tight with high probability. That qualification matters: the guarantee is probabilistic, reflecting the randomized construction. The authors then turn the bounds into a learning approach by optimizing them as objectives for fitting latent-variable models.

The empirical evaluation considers sigmoid belief networks on vision and language benchmarks, with a neural network approximating the posterior. The authors report improvements on these datasets. The contribution therefore joins two aspects of approximate inference: controlling the quality of a likelihood bound and using that bound to learn model parameters. The experiments provide evidence for the approach in the specified model family and application domains.
neurips-2016-variational-bayes-on-monte-.tldr: Random projections produce marginal log-likelihood bounds that are tight with high probability and improve learning in evaluated sigmoid belief networks.

paragraphs: A single image can be consistent with several possible next moments. This paper treats future-frame synthesis probabilistically, allowing one model to generate multiple possible next frames from the same input. The goal is to represent plausible variation in what happens next while accounting for both image content and motion.

The proposed Cross Convolutional Network gives these two kinds of information different representations. It encodes the image as feature maps and encodes motion as convolutional kernels used to help synthesize future frames. This structure links a representation of the scene's appearance with a representation of how it could change.

The authors report good performance on synthetic examples, including two-dimensional shapes and animated game sprites, and on real-world video. They also demonstrate application to visual analogy-making and analyze the learned representations. These findings support the network as a way to model visual dynamics across the tested data types. Its probabilistic formulation is central because the output is a set of possible futures, rather than a single predetermined continuation.
neurips-2016-visual-dynamics-probabilist.tldr: Cross Convolutional Networks combine image features with motion kernels to generate multiple plausible next frames from a single image.
